opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really exciting time. I'd say physics-based computing is kind of a big tent right now. You've got the analog computing folks, the neuromorphic people, optical computing, quantum computing, which is where I came from, and then what we're doing on the thermodynamic side. For a long time these were all fairly siloed communities, each convinced their substrate was the one true path beyond digital.

What I see happening now is a convergence around a shared realization: the digital paradigm, where you fight noise and spend enormous amounts of energy to keep bits perfectly deterministic, is hitting real physical limits. Moore's law is slowing, Dennard scaling ended a while ago, and at the same time the demand for AI compute is exploding. So people are going back to first principles and asking, what does physics naturally want to compute? How do we stop fighting nature and start harnessing it?

In quantum computing, the bet was that you could harness coherence and entanglement, but that requires extreme isolation from the environment, which is very hard at scale. Coming out of that world, my view was: what if instead of fighting noise, you embrace it? Thermal fluctuations are free. Stochasticity is everywhere in nature. And a lot of what we actually want from AI is probabilistic: sampling from distributions, reasoning under uncertainty, generative modeling. So there's a really natural match between noisy physical systems and probabilistic machine learning.

That said, I think the community has a bit of a credibility problem historically. There have been many waves of "this new substrate will replace GPUs," and most didn't pan out, because the digital stack, with all its software, tooling, and economies of scale, is an incredibly strong incumbent. So the challenge for all of us isn't just building a cool physical device. It's building the full stack: the hardware, the algorithms that are native to that hardware, and the software so ML practitioners can actually use it. You have to co-design the algorithms with the physics.

Overall, I'm optimistic. There's more talent, more capital, and more openness to unconventional ideas than there has been in decades, partly because the energy constraints of AI are so obvious now. I think we'll see a Cambrian explosion of different substrates, and the market will figure out which ones are best for which workloads. It probably won't be one winner. It'll be a heterogeneous ecosystem, and I think that's healthy.

r001.rationale: The response says the communities were “fairly siloed,” which clearly characterizes them as fragmented.

r002.rationale: It describes convergence and co-designing algorithms with a substrate’s physics, but does not identify potential to transfer tools between approaches with different physical substrates.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the physics-based computing community is honestly still pretty small, but it's growing fast, and I think it's one of the most exciting corners of the whole computing landscape right now. The way I'd frame it is that for about seventy years we've been building computers by taking physics and basically fighting it. We take a transistor, which is fundamentally an analog, noisy, thermodynamic device, and we spend enormous amounts of energy forcing it to behave like an abstract, deterministic bit. Every time you flip a bit you're dumping a bunch of energy as heat just to suppress the physics underneath. And that's worked incredibly well while Moore's law was carrying us, but we're hitting walls now, both in terms of energy and in terms of how far we can keep shrinking things.

So the physics-based computing crowd, and this includes people doing thermodynamic computing, probabilistic computing, neuromorphic stuff, analog, and of course quantum, are all asking a version of the same question: what if instead of fighting the physics, you let the physics do the computation for you? Nature is already running a massive parallel computation all the time. Particles are sampling from distributions, systems are relaxing to equilibrium, free energy is being minimized. Those are exactly the operations that modern machine learning cares about. Sampling, optimization, linear algebra, matrix inversions. So the bet is that you can build hardware where the native dynamics of the device are the algorithm, rather than a simulation of the algorithm.

What I find really interesting about the community sociologically is that it's a convergence point. You've got people coming from quantum information, from condensed matter, from statistical mechanics, from neuroscience, and from the ML side, and they're all landing on similar ideas from different directions. Quantum computing kind of paved the way culturally, because it got people comfortable with the idea that a computer doesn't have to be a digital von Neumann machine. But I think a lot of us came out of the quantum world and realized that there's this whole middle ground. You don't necessarily need coherence and entanglement to get a big advantage. Just harnessing noise and thermal fluctuations, which digital computers treat as the enemy, can get you a lot for things like Bayesian inference or generative modeling.

There's still a lot of healthy debate in the community, to be clear. People argue about what the actual advantage is, how you quantify it, whether you can scale these things, how you deal with precision and calibration. And there are old scars, because analog computing has had false starts before. But I think the difference now is the demand side. AI is eating the world, and it's incredibly energy hungry, and a huge fraction of what it does is fundamentally stochastic. So for the first time there's a real economic pull for hardware that is natively probabilistic. That changes everything. It's gone from being a fun academic curiosity to something that could actually matter for how we build intelligence at scale.

r001.rationale: It describes the field as a convergence point whose groups arrive at similar ideas, but does not say its subcommunities communicate little with one another.

r002.rationale: It lists approaches built on different physical substrates and their shared goals, but does not identify transferring tools between those approaches as a potential.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a community bringing physics back into the way we think about computation. We often work at a level of abstraction where the hardware is just something that executes an algorithm. But computation is a physical process, and the dynamics of the substrate can do useful work for you.

There are quite different approaches under that umbrella—analog computing, photonics, neuromorphic systems, quantum computing. They don’t all solve the same problems, but they share this question: can we design the computation around what a physical system does naturally, instead of forcing everything into the same digital architecture?

The challenge is making that advantage survive at the level of a complete system. You have to account for control, noise, getting data in and out, and whether people can actually program the thing. That’s where I think the most interesting work is: connecting beautiful physical ideas to useful computational machinery.

r001.rationale: The response lists several distinct approaches under a shared umbrella, but does not say their subcommunities communicate little with one another.

r002.rationale: It says different physical approaches share a question and can exploit their substrates, but does not identify transferring tools between approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a community asking a very fundamental question: what does it mean to compute with a physical system? We tend to abstract away the hardware and think in terms of algorithms, but the computation is happening in matter, with constraints on energy, time, and information flow.

And there are different ways of approaching that. You can use physics to build better computers, or you can use ideas from computation to understand physical systems. What I find exciting is where those directions meet—where the dynamics of the system become part of how you solve the problem. The challenge is turning that into something useful while accounting for the cost of controlling the system and reading out the answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes different approaches and where they meet, but does not say the community is fragmented or that its subcommunities communicate little.

r002.rationale: It mentions using physics to build computers and computation to understand physical systems, but does not identify transferring tools between computing approaches based on different physical substrates.
